LAKE ST, JOSEPH 


SENIOR CAMP. 

On Jnly 16th, the Eleventh Annual Summer 
Camp of the Association for senior members 
will open at Lac St. Joseph, in charge of Mr. H. 
Ballantyne, Educational Secretary. 


For those who have been there no word of }« 


explanation is required. For those: who have 
that pleasant experience still before them a few 
words of description will be acceptable. 

Ten years ago a small party of our members, 


Out-door life is the charm of the camp, 
Tenting, boating, bathing, fishing, exploring 
are the chief means of enjoyment. There are 
facilities also for tennis, base ball, basket ball, 
quoits, ete. In wet weather the club house 
brings the men together and there is no trouble 
in passing the time. 

Plenty of good food, well cooked and served 
at the hands of a competent chef, assure the 
camper that the wants of the inner man will be 


after preliminary exploration, pitched their), swell eared for. 


tents on one of the islands in Lac St. Joseph. 
Their enthusiastic description of their exper- 
iences created wider interest amongst the 
members on their return and led to the acquir- 


ing of the islands for the Association and to'the “ 


establishment of the summer camp at that spot. 

Later, through the efforts of well-known in- 
terested’campers the present splendid log club 
house was erected, and the equipment which 
at first was very small, was enlarged from time 
to time by the addition of tents, boats, etc., 
until the Association now has in addition to the 
club house, a well furnished log kitchen adjoin- 
ing, an ice house, pump, small camp library, 
eight large tents equipped with fly and board 
floor, ten boats, fishing, and swimming 
wharves, etc. 

Through the generosity of Mr. Jas. W. Tester, 
a gasoline launch will be at the disposal of the 
members this year. 

The site of the camp is ideal. Sixty-four 
miles from Montreal to Ste. Agathe, in the 
heart of the Laurentians, and eight miles by road 
brings one to the shores of Lae St. Joseph. On 
a large well-wooded island in the lake the camp, 
is situated. The Association also owns several | 
islands immediately adjoining. 


Speckled trout are the fish of the region, and 
are to be found not only in Lac St. Joseph, but 
more easily in other less visited lakes within 
easy reach of the camp. 

Acamera‘adds greatly tothe pleasure of a visit. 

A vacation at camp means the maximum of 
enjoyment at the minimum of expense. The 
rate for one week, including railway fare and 


drive both ways 18.5... 0... <..2%0¢ $10.00 
Subsequent weeks............-- 5.00 
TORE Ay CLAY Gian sce eis sjetierere satel wip %.00 
Saturday to Monday............ 4.00 


Special rates for entire season and for those 
wishing to camp sepirately. The camp is a 
member’s privilege. The rates represent the 
actual cost of operation with a small margin 
to maintain the camp property. 

The regular days for transportation at cainp 
are going Saturday afternoon, returning Mon- 
day morning. At other times campers will be 
asked to pay a slight additional charge for 
transportation, unless two or more are driving. 
The camp will close September 6th. Further 
information may be had at the office or from 
members of the Camp Committee, as follows: 
B. S. R. Watson, Chairman; Jas. R. Greig, 
W. Jarrett, C. D. Tweedie, H. G. Beall.

4 MEN OF MONTREAL 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT NOTES 


A STRONG TESTIMONY TO THE PHYSICAT, 
DEPARTMENT 


““The success of no Association could be more 
pleasing than that of the Y.M.C.A., which, near 
and far, among the many Christian endeavors of 
the century, is accomplishing the very best 
results among the young men. (In its Athletic 
Department, particularly, is a rational method 
of great excellence and effectiveness being 
pursued, which has for its object not primarily 
the making of prize-winners, but the normal, all- 
rouud development of the individual, that he 
may be the better fitted to make his way in life, 
vigorously, wholesomely. | The Y. M.C.A., in 
point of honest fact, is doing more practical 
good with its athletics than all the athletic clubs 
and colleges combined.’’— Outing. 

Have you joined any of our outdoor clubs yet ? 
The interest is now at its height. The Physical 
Director will be glad to advise with you. 

The Harrier Club Junior and Senior trophies 
won in competition for the championship of the 
city, look fine in our trophy case. Keep it up 
boys. We will soon need a larger case. The 
Harrier Club has set the pace for the other clubs. 

Men interested in track and field events are 
requested to watch for bulletins of the Athletic 
Club. Bi-weekly meets will start soon. 

The Association Foot Ball Club has vacancies 
for a few men. 

The Tennis courts are in use morning and 
evening. Asplendid opportunity for beginners.

FOR THE BOYS. 

The business boys use the Base Ball Park 
Tuesday and Thursday evenings, the school 
boys Monday and Wednesday afternoons and 
Saturday forenoon. Captain Frank Dufty wants 
every fellow who can play ball to come out and 
try for a position on the team, There are some 
good players in sight already. 

The Ste. Agathe Camp Club has had two 
outingsand will have time for a third before 
camp opens, All have had a good time, Come 
on Saturday, June rth. 

The Summer Camp opens at Lac St. Joseph 
for business boys June 18th, and for school 
boys July 2nd. Think fora moment what that 
means! Two weeks of solid enjoyment in one 
of the prettiest spots in Canada, 
boating, 
swimming, 
fishing,

Kvery boy who is going must make application 
accompanied by $2.00 deposit not later than 
June 16th, for the business boys’ camp, and June 
30th, for the school boys’ camp. The rate for 
two weeks is $11.00, which covers everything, 
including railway fare. The camp will be in 
charge of Mr. C. M. Daggett, assisted by a group 
of adult leaders. The camp has now been in 
operation for ten years, during which we have 
had no accidents of any kind nor any serious 
illuess. Parents who are thinking of sending 
their boy, to camp have the assurance that the 
same unremitting care will be exercised in this 
as in previous years. Camp prospectus on ap-

EDUCATIONAL NOTES. 

It is stated that only one person in eight 
completes a Public or High School education, 
and only one in fifteen hundred completes a 
University course. The need created by these 
conditions is being met to an increasing extent 
each year by the evening classes of our own 
Association. ‘These classes fill a distinet field 
of uscfulness, and in no way duplicate the work 
of other agencies. 

Pied Goa) ota 
men who 
attend our 
classes are 
usually older 


than those in 
other even- 
ing schools, 
the average 
age in or 
classes being 
about 25. 

2. There 
are groups of 
menenzaged 
in industrial 
pursuits who 
desirespecial 
training in 
their own 
linesof work. 
Aavis; tHe 
Association 
seeks to pro- 
vide, 

3. Our classes provide special advantages in 
the way of individual instruction. The man 
who has been out of school for some years finds 
difficulties in applying himself to study, and in 
the mastery of various branches which the 
personal encouragement and sympathetic direc- 
tion of the teacher largely overcome. 

The Educational Committee is meeting reg- 
ularly, and carefully planning next season’s 
work. They invite suggestions from our mem- 
bers concerning courses of study, etc. 

The Saturday and Sunday meetings will be 
held regularly during the summer months We 
are glad to welcome at these meetings many 
visitors and strangers. We trust that many of 
ourmembers who are prevented from coming at 


other seasons will find it convenient to do so 
now.

Vou. I. JUNE, 1904, No. 6 


OUR GENERAL SECRETARY 

Mr. and Mrs. Budge sailed from San 
Francisco on May 26th for Sydney, Australia, 
from which city they will visit the principal 
Associations in that country and New Zealand. 
Their departure from Montreal was rendered 
very pleasant by the scenes in connection with 
the Annual Meeting. 

At the tea preceding, Mrs. Budge was pre- 
sented with a beautiful bouquet of flowers by 
Mr. Wm. Hayes, Chairman of the Sunday 
Afternoon Class, who fittingly expressed the 
feeling of the members in a short speech. 

At the Annual Meeting which followed, Mr. 
Budge was the recipient, on behalf of himself 
and Mrs. Budge, of a handsome silver fruit 
service, together with a purse from the Board of 
Directors and friends. Mr. Kingman, who 
made the presentation, spoke in the warmest 
terms of Mr. Budge’s thirty years as secretary, 
and of the blessing which had rested upon his 
labors. . 

‘The best wishes and prayers of many friends 
will accompany Mr. and Mrs. Budge on their 
journey. é 


ANNUAL REPORTS. 

Instead of issuing a separately printed Annual 
Report, the Directors decided to publish the 
same in the present issue of ‘‘ Men of Montreal,’’ 
which contains the Annual Report of the Board, 
the Treasurer’s statement, list of subscribers, and 
reports of Committees. These will all repay a 
careful reading. 

“Men of Montreal’’ will not appear again 
until September. That number will contain the 
names of the Officers, Directorsand Commiittee- 
men, together with illustrated anuouncement of 
the work for the fall and winter. 


VISITORS 

Among recent visitors to our Association were 
Dr. A. G. Studer, Secretary of the Association 
in Detroit, Michigan, who is an old Montreal 
boy, and whose parents live in this city ; Mr. 
W. M. Danner, Secretary of the Association in 
Denver, Colorado, and Mr, N. M. MacChesney, 
Assistant General Secretary of the Chicago 
Association. 


A TRIBUTE FROM A FRIEND 
The following lines from the pen of Mr. 
Warburton, who was our guest at the annual 
tea, will be read with interest in view of Mr. 
Budge’s completion of thirty years in the Sec- 
retaryship of the Montreal Association, and of 
his visit to Australasia in the interests of the 
Associations in those countries. 
To Mr. Budge 
To live for others, pouring into mind and heart 


The truest light; to cause the candles of the 
Lord to burn 


In the dim places; to waken music where harsh 
Discord clanged before; to drive 
The bats of sorrow out, and fill the life with 


song birds; 

To lead the wayward feet back, tremblingly, 
but 

With full consent of will, to paths of virtue and 
of peace; 


To help men see in Jesus their true Friend 

By showing them what true, deep friendship is; 

To live a sweet and gracious life, full of all 
charity ;— 

And thus to grow into the very hearts of men 

Until they love you like a brother— 

This is true living and worth while. 

And we to-night would tell you, friend, 

How deep our love is for you, 

And join you in His praise, who for these years 

Has been your Model, Master, Helper, Guide. 

We bid you Godspeed as you turn to-night 

Your well-known face toward the Golden Gate 

To cross the vast Pacific, and to find 

In distant countries other friends to love. 

We bid you God-speed, and every fav’ring gale 

Shall bear from us to you our hearts’ true love. 

And it will cheer you in the distant land 

To know that here we pray that God will bless 

And help you there, and in due time 

Bring you safe home again. 

If love and prayer will make a pleasant journey 

Yours, our friend, shall be 

Filled to the full with sweet felicity. 


MILITIA CAMP 
The Association tent will be placed in the 
Militia Camp,” which opens this year at La- 
prairie, June 28th. Mr. Arthur F. Bell will be 
in charge. 
GLEE CLUB 
The Glee Club has discontinued practices for 
the summer, but will resume early in the 
fall, when an effort will be made to organize a 
Banjo and Guitar Club as well. 
THE ENTERTAINMENT COURSE 
Last season was so much enjoyed by our 
members that the committee have decided to 
arrange an Entertainment Course of eight 
numbers for the coming falland winter months.

THE BUFFALO CONVENTION 


Sixteen hundred and twenty-eight delegates 
from the United States and Canada attended the 
Thirty-fifth International Convention at Buffalo, 
May rith to 15th. It was one of the most 
remarkable and important conventions of recent 
years. The reports presented indicate that the 
growth of the Association in the three years 
since the Jubilee at Boston, has been greater 
than in the ten years preceding. Inspiring ad- 
dresses by Dr. Barbour of Rochester, Dr. G,. 
Campbell Morgan, Robert E. Speer and others, 
made never-to-be-forgotten impressions. Best 
of all, the difficult questions arising out of the 
relation of the International and State Com- 
mittees were satisfactorily adjusted. 

The following extract from an article by Rev. 
James IL, Barton, D.D., in ‘‘ The Congrega- 
tionalist,’’ is worth repeating :— 

‘“ Upon one attending such a convention for 
the first time several impressions are made. 

1. That a surprising number of the ‘“ young 
men’? are remarkably bald or gray. It seems 
as if the principle, ‘‘once a young man always 
a young man,’’ dominates the society and gives 
it permanent strength. The interesting part of 
it is that no one seems to think them old. 

2. That if the men who took prominent part 
in the debate received their training in the 
Association it must be one of the best debating 
schools in the world, 


3. That an Association that can command the 
time and strength of so many high railroad and 
bank officials and leading men in political and 
professional careers, as well as all departments 
of business, must have vital power destined to 
accomplish great things. 

4. That the underlying and fundamental 
principle and idea of the Association is to reach 
young men in this land and in every land and 
bring them to a saving knowledge of Jesus 
Christ, 

5. That laymen can teach theologians how to 
settle a hot controversy and not sacrifice mutual 
confidence and affection. 

6. That the best way to unite denominations 
is not to debate plans for union but to go to 
work together for a common cause. 

7. That however much Presbyterians may 
believe in the presbytery and Methodists in the 
episcopacy, when they get thoroughly warmed 
up in debate and forget their ecclesiastical 
affiliations, they can set forth with convincing 
eloquence the necessity of maintaining the 
absolute independence of the local association. 

8. That the Young Men’s Christian Associa- 
tion is in the hands of wise leaders, commands 
the confidence of splendid people in all denom- 
inations and has a distinctive field at home and 
abroad for its operations.”’ 


8 MEN OF MONTREAL 


MEN FROM THE EAST 
Messrs. John R. Mott, of New York, E. C. 
Carter, National Secretary for India, Galen M. 
lisher, National Secretary for Japan, and F. §. 
Irockinan, National Secretary for China, visited 
our Association on May 18th last, and were our 
guests at an impromptu social gathering of our 
Directors and other friends that evening. Their 
interesting and inspiring words concerning the 
progress of the Association in foreign lands 
made a profound impression. The gathering 
was unique, in that we had the leading Associa- 
tion Secretaries from the three great countries 
of India, China and Japan, together with Mr. 
Mott, whose earnest efforts for young men have 
been so largely blessed. We are hopeful that 
Mr, Brockman and Mr. Fisher will be able to 

visit us again during their furlough. 


RAILROAD DEPARTMENT NOTES. 

Baths are very popular. 

Four new tubs are to be installed immediately. 

Summer membership has been authorized by 
the Committee of Management. 

The class in Vocal Music is making excellent 
progress under Mr, H, Judson Morse. 

Although business is very slack on the rail- 
road at present, the number of beds used is on 
the increase, 

The Base Ball Club have secured good 
grounds for the summer and are getting uni- 
forms and equipment, The club has been 
adinitted to the league. 

Secretary A. S. McAlister, of Island Pond, Vt., 
addressed the Sunday afternoon meeting. Good 
music was furnished by the Glee Club and a 
Male Quartette. 

Ir. J. Sissons, our popular Chef, and his 
assistant, Mr. Conroy, have contracted to fur- 
nish refreshments at the Grand Trunk Boating 
Club during the Summer, 

At the close of the Base Ball Club Concert, in 
library Hall, Friday Evening, May 2i1st., a 
beautiful Teacher's Bible was presented to Mr. P. 
A. Doig, who is leaving our Association to take 
up the work at the City Association. The 
presentation was made by Ass’t Sec'y Pugh, on 
behalf of the young men. 

A rare opportunity is being offered for young 
men to learn telegraphy. Our classes are con- 
ducted six nights a week during the entire year, 
under conipetent instructors, besides which the 
rooms are open for practice at any hour of the 
day. 

The demand is great for telegraph operators, 
and young men are constantly being taken from 
the key to fill positions as Train Dispatchers 
and Station Agents and offices of greater im- 
portance,

MEN OF MONTREAL 9 


53rd ANNUAL REPORT 


OF THE 


Young Men’s Christian Association 
OF THE CITY OF MONTREAL. 


INCORPORATED 
DEC. 1870. 


ORGANIZED 
NOV. 1851. 


PRESENTED AT THE ANNUAL MEETING HELD ON TUESDAY 
EVENING, MAY oth, Igo4. 


The Fifty-third Annual Meeting of the Association was held on ‘Tuesday 
evening, May roth, 1904, at 8 o’clock, in the Lecture Hall. Mr. Robt. Munro, 
President, occupied the chair. Devotional exercises were conducted by Rev. 
Robert Johnston, D.D., pastor of the American Presbyterian Church. 

The minutes of the previous meeting were accepted as read. 

The Fifty-third Annual Report of the Board of Directors was then read by 
Mr. Budge, and the Financial Statement of the Association presented by Mr. 
lL. H. Packard, Treasurer. 

Mr. C. T. Williams presented the report of the Committee on Vacancies, 
nominating the following gentlemen as Directors for the ensuing three years : 

D. W. Ross Jas. W. Knox H. B. Ames 
C. T. Williams D. Bentley G. H. Harrower 

There being no other nominations these gentlemen were declared elected. 

The Report of the Railroad Branch, at Point St. Charles, was presented by 
Mr. Thos. McHattie, Treasurer. 

On motion, these reports were adopted, and ordered to be printed and 
circulated among the members and subscribers of the Association. 

A cordial vote of thanks was also tendered to the ladies, the press, and all 
who had in any way contributed to the success of the work during the year. 

A very pleasing event then occurred, when Mr. Abner Kingman, on behalf 
of the Board of Directors, called the attention of the members to the fact that 
Mr. Budge has recently completed thirty years of active service as Secretary of 
the Association, and after speaking in high terms of his work as Secretary, on 
behalf of the Directors and friends, presented Mr. and Mrs. Budge witha beautiful 
silver fruit service, together with a purse for their approaching journey to Australia. 

After further short addressesfrom Mr. C. I. Williams and Rey. Dr. Johnston, 
Mr. Budge replied with words of thanks and reminiscences of his early connection 
with the Association. 

The meeting adjourned with the hymn, ‘‘ Blest be the Tie that Binds.”’ 


10 MEN OF MONTREAL 


ANNUAL REPORT 
OF THE 


BOARD OF DiRECTORS. 


In submitting the detailed report of the work of another year to the mem- 
bers of the Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal, the Board of 
Directors desire to record— 


1. Their appreciation of the sympathetic and loyal co-operation of a 
larger number of committee men and volunteer workers than in any previous 
year. 


2. The unselfish devotion of the members of the staff to the interests of 
the Association. 


3. The ever-increasing confidence of the business men and citizens in 
the aims and also in the general administration of the affairs of the Associa- 
tion. It is no longer regarded as a private institution, but as a public bene- 
factor, and an absolute necessity in the increasing complexity of modern city 


life. 


4. The unity of the Directors in the consideration of the affairs of the 
Association, and, above all, the abundant blessing of God upon the whole 
work. 


From a careful study of the reports of departments to be submitted 
to-night it will be seen— 


1. Membership.—That 780 new members joined the Association during 
the year, that 60 per cent. of the members renewed, that young men from all 
classes and business interests are drawn to the membership, that the various 
denominations are proportionately represented, and that the receipts from 
fees were larger than in any previous year, viz.,7$8,673.80. 

There are many who think that the fee for seniors should be increased, 
that the regular ticket should be placed at $2.00, and an added charge of $5.00 
for the physical department, similar to the class tuition, which are added to 
those entering the evening classes. This important question will have the 
careful consideration of the Membership Committee and the Board. 


2. Educational.—The educational classes show a total individual enrol- 
ment of 463 members, which is an advance of 27 over last year. A spring 
term has been added, with an enrolment of 61 members. Nine educational 
lectures were given, with an attendance of 1,175 men, and a Canadian Club 
added with 40 members. 


3. Religious.—The religious department shows a more complete organ- 
ization in its Bible study and foreign work than heretofore, and a more in- 
telligent and effective effort to make permanent the results which have grown 
out of the religious meetings and Bible study classes. The names of 226 
young men have been sent to the city pastors during the year. In this 
practical way the Association seeks to co-operate with the church in its 
mission towards young men. 


MEN OF MONTREAL ll 


4. Physical—The expansion of the physical work has only been limited 
by the size of the gymnasium and the locker room accommodation. ‘Twenty- 
seven class sessions each week have been conducted, with a total enrolment 
of 991. The department clubs have grown both in members and efficiency. 
The clubs now number twelve. A most helpful spirit prevails among the 
500 members, who are taking advantage of this attractive opportunity. 


5. Social—A marked advance is apparent in the social life and spirit 
which prevails in and around the building. This has resulted from the 
better supervision of this department, the addition of a popular course of 
entertainments, the multiplication of teas for groups of members in confer- 
ence over the work, and the securing of an increasing number of interested 
members as tenants in the rented rooms in the building. 

The addition of a Glee Club and Chess Club has been most helpful, and 
also the social song service after church on Sunday evenings. The Strangers’ 
Tea on Sunday evening has been better organized, and 128 members have 
joined the Association through this agency. 


6. Boys.—The work on behalf of boys shows a membership of 231, 
with 85 serving on various committees. The attendance at the religious 
meetings shows a marked increase, and pledges for $60.00 have been made 
towards the foreign work. 

One of the most gratifying features of this most important department 
has been the development of the boys in sharing the responsibility for the 
work. This will have an important bearing upon their own future as well 
as the future of the Association work. One of the members from this de- 
partment will join the staff this summer in preparation for the secretaryship. 


7. Summer Camp.—The summer vacation camp showed a decrease in 
attendance last season. This was accounted for by the fact that the business 
boys’ camp was not held, that the season was unusually wet and unattractive 
for camping, and that the committee depended too largely on the success of 
past years. For this season there will be an additional attraction of a 
handsome gasoline launch, kindly donated by Mr. J. W. Tester, and both 
senior and junior committees have matters well in hand for a successful 
season. 

A permanent wharf and boat house is a great necessity. Here is an 
opportunity for some friends of the Association to make this addition to the 
equipment of this ideal vacation resort. 


8. ‘Men of Montreal.”—On January Ist an eight-page paper was issued 
that members and subscribers might be acquainted with the current news of 
the work. Your Directors believe this to be a valuable means of informing 
the friends of the Association of its current work. Members are invited to 
suggest names to those to whom it might be sent. The question of making 
this a four-page weekly has been discussed. For purposes of announcement 
of events of the week it would be of greater value. 


9. Railroad Branch.—The special feature of the work of the past year 
was the completion of the Railway Men’s Building at Point St. Charles. This 
was opened January 21st. The entire cost is no yetffully adjusted, but it will 
be about $42,000. This branch is not only intended for the use of the 
employees of the Grand Trunk Railway, but for all the young men resident 
in that section of the city. It contains physical, educational, social, dormitory 
and restaurant privileges. Its present membership is 396, and it will be 
largely increased next fall. The results already secured through its religious 
meetings are most encouraging. 


10. Militia Camp.—For ten days in July, 1903, this As-ociation undertook 
the charge of a tent in the Militia Camp at Three Rivers, at the request of 
the Provincial Committee. Three thousand volunteers were under canvas. . 
Reading and writing room, games, social privileges and religious meetings 
were maintained with the most encouraging results. The Association tent 
became not only the counter attraction to the saloon and canteen, but was 
the popular resort for the men during camp, and proved a means of escape 


for many a young man under severe temptation. This work will be carried 
on again this year, 


11. Finances.—A growing work always demands increased expenditure. 
The Association has three sources of income—rentals, fees and subscriptions. 
The finincial statement will show that the income from 1entals aud fees have 
been maintained and slightly increased, but that the revenue from subscrip- 
tions decreased. The cause has been exceptional. The death of several of 
our largest annual contributors, and inability of others to give as in former 
years, has caused a loss of over $1,000. This has been met in part by new 
subscriptions. But the Finance Committee feel convinced that a large num- 
ber of new subscriptions could be secured by a more careful and thorough 
study of the field, and in order to meet the demands for extension of the 
work which now presses upon us, $10,000 should be secured for subscriptions 
instead of $7,000, as at present. This will be the task which the Finance 
Committee will be asked to undertake during the coming year. 


12. Future Plans and Opportunities.—The Association las now passed the 
stage of experiment. It is recognized as an absolute necessity in the city 
life of young men. Its permanent value is unquestioned by any thoughtful 
person. Therefore, the time has come to wisely plan for the future needs 
of the city. Last year your Directors suggested a forward movement. Some 
progress has been made, but aggressive action was delayed so as not to inter- 
fere with the canvas for the McGill College Association Building, which, we 
are glad to hear, is now assured, $95,000 having been subscribes. 

We congratulate the College Association on this splendid result—the 
prospective completion of the building within a year. 


Your Directors would present the following plans for the future :— 


1. The Annex to the Dominion Square Building.—The plans for this 
Annex are well under way by the special committee. It is estimated that 
the purchase of the additional land required and the completion of the build- 
ing will cost $125,000. This will give a separate,equipment for the Boys’ 
Department, an enlarged gymnasium and locker room, an enlarged hall on 
the ground floor, a modern equipment for the library and evening classes, a 
restaurant, and seventy additional rooms for rental to members. These 
increased privileges would accommodate 4,009 members, and there would 
seem to be little difficulty in holding that membership at this central point. 
The increased fees and rentals would pay the added fixed charges. Work on 
this should be begun not later than May Ist, 1995. 


2. East End.—A call has come from the Ezst End. The addition of 
large factories and shops employing thousands of men makes this urgent. 
There is no suitable building for rental available. A new building would 
require to be erected. The land would cost $3,000, and a building sufficient 
to begin with, having plans for extension as the work would warrant, would 


MEN OF MONTREAL 


cost from $8,000 to $12,000. If some friend would purchase the land and 
hold it for. the Association, and another erect the building, this urgent call 
would be met. Amount required, $15,000. 


3. Special Fund.—A special fund for the conduct of religious work by 
means of lectures and addresses to men, and by the extension of Bible teach- 
ing amongst the young men of Montreal. 


4. Athletic Field—An athletic field with equipment. Amount required, 
$20,000. 


5. Branch.—Branches for work for boys in Westmount, and in the 
North East End. 


6. Library.—The enlargement of the present library to 10,000 volumes, 
and an endowment to provide for its care and development. 


7. Permanent Fund.—Permanent endowment. ‘This should be largely 
increased. Contributions invited. The interest to be used in the exten- 
sion of the work as the judgment of the Directors may determine. 


BEQUESTS. 


During the past year we have been notified of two bequests—(1) By the 
will of the late A. I’. Gault, $1,000; (2) of the late James Cooper; the Associa- 
tion is one of three other institutions which share in the residue of his estate. 
We are also advised of $1,009 which will come to the Association through 
the will of the late Francis Scholes. 

To those who have a sense of their responsibility in the disposition of 
their money, the choice of channels of benevolence is often one of difficulty. 
They desire to direct their money where it will accomplish the largest prac- 
tical good, and they feel a sense of responsibility for the city where their 
money has been made and their life has been spent. In this connection we 
beg to suggest the Young Men’s Christian Association of the City of Montreal. 


1. For Permanency.—The Association is an incorporated body. The 
Directors are business men—representatives of the evangelical churches of 
the city. Funds can be held in the name and to the credit of the donor. 


2. The diversity of the objects to which funds may be applied. (See 
list above). 


3. The fact that this work so largely deals with young men whose lives 
are in process of formation. It makes for righteousness. It reaches all 
classes of young men and all creeds. It offers an opportunity for the young 
men who seek self-improvement. It has a close relation to the commercial 
and mechanical interests of the city. It is elastic and practical in its efforts 
to meet the needs of men as they arise. It is in no sense hide-bound. 


4. It is economical because it is preventive. At the same time it stands 
for reformation and reconstruction of life on the only possible basis. Its 
| 
past work is a guarantee of its future. 


5. It is a profitable investment because its buildings are open and its 
work continued during 365 days of each year, and fourteen to sixteen hours 
of each day. There is no lost time. 


14 MEN OF MONTREAL 


There can be no more important class to save and train for the future 
of the church, the city and the community than the young men upon whom 
these responsibilities are to.rest. There is no class so wrecked and ruined 
by temptation. Therefore the Directors confidently appeal to the business 
men, the ladies of the city, and the young men to carefully consider this pro- 
position for wise investment—present or future—and thus make possible and 
permanent an increasingly enlarged and effective work for the boys and 
young men of this city, who will be passing along in constant procession in 


the days to come. 
The person who helps to meet the present need, and thus share the joys 
of seeing the results accomplished, is surely following the wisest course. 


ROBERT MUNRO, D. A. BupGE, 
President. Secretary.

the honorary membership has been elimin-

RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT. 

The Department Committee has met regu- 
larly since January, and carefully reviewed 
the work so efficiently carried on by the 
various sub-committees in immediate charge 
of the meetings and Bible classes. 

The Saturday Night Meeting Committee 
was reorganized in November with good re- 
sults. The total attendance at the meeting 
during the year was 2,594; average, 50. We 
wish more of our members would plan to 
attend the meeting, not only for the help 
they might receive, but for that which they 
might render others. The meeting has con- 
tinued to be a training ground and a great 
means of help to those beginning the Chris- 
tian life, and fills a place of the highest im- 
portance in the Association. 

The Meeting for Men on Sunday afternoon 
at four o’clock was continued from October 
to May; total attendance, 8,387; average, 
239. The attendance shows a slight in- 
crease over last year, and encouraging pro- 
gress has been made. The Male Quartette, 
together with other friends, rendered very 
efficient and attractive musical service. 

Special interest attached to the visits of 
Rev. William Patterson, of Philadelphia ; 
Dr. L. B. Sperry, of Oberlin; Mr. George 
Sherwood Eddy, of India; Mr. Fred. B. 
Smith, of New York, and Mr. Chas. Inglis, 
of London, England. The names of over 
one hundred and eighty young men were re- 
ceived as inquirers concerning the Christian 
life, a large number of whom have since 
shown their sincerity by uniting with the 
church and in other ways. 

The Sunday Afternoon Bible Class had a 
total attendance of 3,341; average, 66 per 
Sunday. From May to October the class 
studied “Lessons from Old Testament Char- 
acters,’ and in November commenced with 
studies in the Acts of the Apostles. These 
studies have been followed with close atten- 
tion, and have been very profitable. The 
Ccmmittee have again to report that a num- 
ber of members have taken up Sunday school 
work during the year. On Sunday, January 
17th, 86 old and new members joined in a 
class tea, followed by brief testimony from 
each member. It was inspiring to find that 
we had members from Japan, Russia, Aus- 
tralia, Barbadoes, etc., besides the countries 
nearer home and Great Britain. Mr. Budge, 
the leader of the class, was presented with a 
handsome Topical Bible as a token of the 


MEN OF 


MONTREAL 19 


esteem in which he is held by the members 
of the class. The committee have received 
letters from members stating how their at- 
tendance at the class had helped them to lead 
a Christian 1** Twenty-seven of our 
members have ..aen up the Daily Study of 
the Bible on the plan of the “Morning 
Watch.” The class appreciates the faithful 
services of Mr. W. T. Walmsley, at the piano, 
and Mr. Harry Griffiths as leader of the 
singing. 

The Gymnasium Men's Bible Study Club, 
under the leadership of Mr. Merritt, our 
Physical Director, held 30 sessions, with an 
average attendance of 39. This class is one 
of the distinctively encouraging features of 
the department. 

The BHducational Department Bible Class 
met on Tuesday evening, under the leader- 
ship of Mr. Ballantyne, with an average of 
13. This class is mainly attended by stu- 
dents in the educational department, and fills 
an exceedingly useful place in the lives of 
the men. 

The Tuesday Evening Bible Classes were 
organized for the season, commencing No- 
vember 17th. We are again indebted to 
Rey. J. L. Gilmour. for a very interesting and 
profitable course of lessons on “The Old 
Testament Prophets.” 

Mr. Budge conducted a series of twenty 
studies on “Personal Work,” which have 
greatly stimulated interest on the part of 
Christian men in the welfare of others. 


A third group of men followed a normal 
ccurse in “The Teaching of Bible C! ‘sas,” 
condueted by Mr. Calhoun. Severn’ men 
followed this course preparatory to taking 
up Bible class work in Sunday schools, and 
the other members of the class who are en- 
gaged regularly in teaching find the class of 
great service. 

On April 26th a reunion of Bible class stu- 
dents was held, at which announcement was 
‘made of the courses of study for next year. 
Short addresses were delivered by Rev. J. L. 
Gilmour and Rev. Dr. Johnston, which great- 
ly encouraged those present to continue and 
enlarge their efforts in this direction. 

The Foreign Work Committee was reor- 
ganized early in the fall, preparatory to the 
visit of Mr. John R. Mott on October Ist, at 
which about $750.00 was pledged towards the 
work for boys in Calcutta, under the super- 
vision of the International Committee. On 
March 19-20 we had the pleasure of a visit 
from Mr. George Sherwood Eddy, when a 
further sum of about $300.00 was added, 
which brought the fund up to over $1,400.00. 
It is the intention of the committee to raise 
$1,200.00 annually for this purpose A- great 
stimulus has come into the lives of many of 
our members through the privilege of shar- 
ing in this important work for those in less 
favored lands. 


The Week of Prayer was profitably ob- 
served, Nov. 8-15, by meetings for prayer 
each evening at 9.30. 

On October 8th Rey. Dr. .. Balecom Shaw, 
of New York, addressed a gathering of 
workers on the question of personal effort 
for others. The occasion was a distinct 
privilege. 

The meetings conducted by Dr. Sperry, 
Dec. 6-11, were largely attended, and proved 
exceedingly profitable. The average at- 
tendance for the week was 377 men. These 
addresses dealt with the question of the phy- 
sical life of men as related to Christian life 
and character. 

Short informal services have been held 
each Sunday morning at the Western Hos- 
pital under the direction of a small commit- 
tee, and these have been exceedingly appre. 
ciated by the patients. Visitation of sick 
young men has been made in the other hos-- 
pitals in the city. Through the kindness ot 
our Ladies’ Committee, we have been able 
to send flowers to many who were without 
ministrations of this kind. 

During the latter part of the winter the 
parlors were opened at 8.30 on Sunday even- 
ings, in charge of the Secretaries, for an in- 
formal service of sacred song, This action 
met with deep appreciation on the part of 
many young men, who were thus enabled to 
spend the evening profitably in the building. 

The Committee recommend, after careful 
consideration, that next season the Men's 
Meeting and Sunday Afternoon Bible Class 
be interchanged—the Men's Meeting to -be 
held at 3 o’clock, followed by the Bible Class 
at 4.30. It is felt that this arrangement will 
prove a better order, and yield larger results. 
During the year the names of 230 young men 
have been sent to pastors, with a view of 
their being invited to the various services of 
the church, and the names of those who have 
been specially interested in the Christian life 
as the result of the meetings and other work 
cr the Association have also been sent to 
pestors. 

The attendance at the various meetings 
end Bible classes during the year has been 
as follows :—

MONTREAL 


SOCIAL COMMITTEE. 


The Social Committee has worked faith- 
fully and earnestly to promote the social 
life of the building, and have kept continu- 
ally in mind some problems of this work 
which will undoubtedly help them during the 
next year. Social events of various kinds 
have been held in the Physical, Hducational 
and Religious Department, over which the 
Committee had no direct oversight, but for 
which assistance was gladly rendered. The 
largest event of the season was the New 
Year’s Reception. About 2,500 people at- 
tended during the afternoon and evening. 
Two illustrated lectures were given, on 
“Canada,” and the “River and Gulf of St. 
Lawrence,” by Mr. I. Gammell and Dr. Kelley 
respectively. The usual Gymnasium exhi- 
bition and the evening Concert were popular 
features. The collection of original draw- 
ings from the Century Company of New 
York, as well as an exhibit of electrical 
novelties, were much appreciated. 

Four parlor socials have been held, with 
about 375 men attending, most of them being 
new members. A Social Song Service in 
the parlors of the building on Sunday even- 
ings after church has brought together from 
20 to 40 men each Sunday, the most of them 
being men living in boarding houses. The 
Committee undertook a course of four con- 
certs which proved very successful. About 
1,300 people, mostly members and their 
friends, attended. This feature has met a 
decided need, and the Committee is now plan- 
ning for a more extensive course next season. 


A Shuffle Board has been purchased for the 
Game Room, and a song card of popular 
songs printed for use on informal occasions. 
The Reception Committee helped with the 
office work, especially during the heavy fall 
months. 

After a lapse of several years, the Chess 
Club is again in existence. At a general 
meeting, held last November, the following 
officers were elected :—President, B. S. R. 
Watson; Vice-President, H. J. Rose; Sec- 
retary-Treasurer, P. C. Moir; Committee, 
J. L. Carnegie, S. Wilson and J. A. Howell. 
The club has a membership of about 25 
players. An interesting handicap tourna- 
ment was held during the winter, which was 
won by Mr. H. J. Rose, Mr. J. A. Howell 
coming second. On invitation of the West- 
mount Chess Club, we played two matches 
with them in their rooms, our club winning 
the first one. 

The Glee Club is composed of 18 members, 


with the following officers :—Leader, C. M. 
Daggett; President and Manager, A. E. 
DesIslets; Sec.-Treas. A. L. McConnell ; 


Committee, F. W. Shaw, H. Ballantyne, Geo. 
W. Stevenson. The club was. organized 
late in the season. and were thus only able 


to appear on five occasions, viz., the Glee 
Club concert, Railroad Association bazaar, 
Educational Class closing, St. Lambert Boat- 
ing Club, Physical Department banquet. 
JAS. 3°. NUTT, 
Chairman. 


Strangers’ Tea. 


The Strangers’ Tea has been in charge of 
a Special Committee, with the assistance of 
one of the Secretaries. The opportunity of 
making men feel at home in the city and 
country, and giving them the benefit of our 
experience, has been a good one, and many 
expressions of thankfulness have come from 
those who have been our guests on these oc- 
easions. One of the Board of Directors has 
presided as often as it was possible, and two 
of the Secretaries have always been present. 
The names of strangers are secured through 
the Employment Bureau, through enquiries 
made for boarding houses and through our 
members. Thirty-seven sessions have been 
held, and 364 men have been present; 128 of 
this number have joined the Association 
direct or by transfer. The following are the 
countries from which the men have come :—

GEO. A. GALL,

SUMMER CAMP. 


The Association Camp at Lac St. Joseph 
is one of our most popular summer attrac- 
tions. It provides opportunities for a pleas- 
ant and healthful vacation, which it would 
be difficult to rival. 

The Boys’ Camp opened on the 27th of 
June, and continued until the 11th of July. 
Forty-nine boys were in attendance, under 
the supervision of a corps of leaders ap- 
pointed by their committee. Sixty senior 
members spent their vacation here, some 
going for two or three days, and others for 
two weeks, from July 11th to September ist. 
Helpful Sunday services were maintained. 

The receipts from the Junior Camp were 
$600.57, and the expenditure $481.43, leaving 
a balance of $119.14. The receipts from the 
Senior Camp were $792.75, and expenditure 
$671.48, leaving a balance of $121.32. At 
the close of the season the sum of $240.46 was 
handed by the two committees to the Per- 
manent Camp. 

The Permanent 
pended $847.66 on 


Camp Committee ex- 
improvements, including 


MEN OF MONTREAL 21 


two new boats, a cooking stove, a pump for 
the purpose of forcing water direct to the 
kitchen, tents, a gasoline launch, etc. Their 
indebtedness to the Association is $432.10. 


R. HENDERSON, 
Chairman. 


EMPLOYMENT DEPARTMENT. 


Most of the applicants for employment 
have been new arrivals in the country, and 
many of them unskilled workmen. Special 
attention has been given to applications of 
our members; 451 applications have been 
received; 174 have secured employment di- 
rectly through our efforts, and many more 
have been introduced to members, which has 
been the means of their eventually securing 
work: 150 letters have been given for this 
purpose ; 193 requests have been received 
frem employers. Many applications for boys 
we were unable to fill. Sixty-seven young 
men have joined the Association through this 
agency. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The membership at date is 231, composed 
of 127 school boys and 104 business boys, as 
compared with 211 for the same date last 
year. This shows an increase of 27, but as 
we had only 164 members last September, we 
feel that a substantial gain has been made. 
Forty-eight boys have continued their mem- 
bership in the Senior Department, and 85 
beys have served on the various committees. 

The Friday Evening Meeting has been held 
regularly throughout the year, with the ex~ 
ception of July and August, and has been 
an encouraging feature of the work. We 
have striven to make the meetings attractive, 
interesting and helpful, keeping ever in mind 
the instruction and development of the boys. 
Special mention should be made of a series 
of talks by the Physical Director, Mr. J. E. 
Merritt, on ‘‘The Boy and His Body.” Alcoho), 
Tobacco and Impurity were dealt with, anda 
their effect upon the body discussed. The 
average attendance at this meeting has been 
44, as compared with 25 last year. 

The younger boys’ meeting, held each Fri- 
day afternoon, was changed into a_ Bible 
Study Club, and conducted by the Secretary. 
This club has been the means of holding ana 
developing a number of boys who soon will 
be able to render valuable service. The 
average attendance has been 35. By means 
of these two meetings we have been able to 
touch over 200 boys in our membership. 

The Song Service every other Sunday 
morning at the General Hospital has been 
held regularly since last October. This has 
proven one of the most successful and most 
appreciated features of our work. It is not 
possible to estimate the effect of this un- 


selfish service on the lives of both patients 
and boys. 

A number of boys have been interested in 
the Bible Classes, conducted by Mr. H. G. 
Beall and the Secretary. The normal course 
preparing older boys to teach has been a spe- 
cial feature of this work. This class was 
started to meet the need of new teachers to 
replace the older workers dropping out. 
These two classes had an enrollment of 26. 
During the year, as far as we have been able 
to find out, 17 boys have been led to decide 
for Christ, and five have united with the 
churches as a result of the work. A strong 
effort has been made to interest the boys in 
systematic giving to Foreign Missions. 
Pledges have been receivea to the extent of 
$60.00 from 55 contributors. 

Two educational classes have been con- 
ducted for Business Boys, one in Shorthand 
and one in Arithmetic, under the supervi- 
sion of the Educational Committee of the 
Association. We would recommend the en- 
fargement of this work in the coming year 
to include more subjects. The enrollment 
was :—Shorthand, 16; Arithmetic, 15 ; aver- 
age attendance, 9 in each class. 

forty-nine new books have been added to ~ 
che Library, which now consists of 600 
volumes. This has been used by a large 
number of the boys. The list of magazines 
on the reading tables was revised at the first 
of the year, and new covers bought. There 
are now 13 magazines on file. 


The social work has been made very pro- 
minent this year. Sixteen small group 
socials have been held. The special features 
were the Annual Sleigh Drive, when 90 boys 
drove around the two Mountains; the Camp 
Reunion, held at the Railway Building at 
Point St. Charles, under the management of 
the Camp Chef, Mr. Sissons; the Birthday 
Social, whereby $13.00 was realized for the 
purchase of new books tor the Library, and 
the Closing Entertainment, at which a large 
number of parentS were present. The 
Junior Ladies’ Committee nas been of great 
assistance in all our social gatherings. The 
various games in the game room have been 
constantly in use. A snuffle-board has been 
added to our equipment and game tourna- 
ments held. 


The average attendance at the gymnasium 
classes has been as follows :— 


Average 
Sessions. Attendance. 
Junior School Boys ...... 87 32 
Senior School Boys ...... 89 17 
Business Boys ........ Yaw Oo. 26

Basket Ball tournaments were conducted 
in three classes, and at the close of these a 
Bowling Tournament was organized for the 
Senior School Boys, and Indoor Hockey was 
played by the Junior School Boys. Several 


22 MEN OF 


MONTREAL 


Basket Ball games with outside teams have 
also been played. During the. winter a 
Hockey Club was organized, and the Minto 
Rink used twice a week. Several snow- 
shoe tramps were also held. 


The Summer Camp was held as usual at 
Lae St. Joseph from June 26th to July 9th, 
and was attended by 49 boys. On account 
of the difficulty in securing proper super- 
vision, it was found necessary to take both 
Business and School Boys in one camp. Mr. 
Harry Ballantyne was in charge, assisted by 
the following efficient corps of leaders :—Dr. 
H. S. Shaw, Messrs. A. E. Shaw, H. H. Patch, 
J. K. Shuttleworth, A. B. Dawson, J. N. 
McCuaig, W. A. Maclaren and C. S. Paterson. 
Excursions, athletic sports, mock trials, elec- 
ticns, boating, swimming, ete., kept the boys 
busily occupied, and all came home without 
any accident. 

The voluntary Bible Class was attended by 
practically all the campers. The Friday 
evening meeting, the Sunday service, and 
evening prayers in the tents helped to sur- 
round the boys with a Christian atmosphere, 
and their lives, we feel sure, were benefitted 
to a great extent. Five boys openly professed 
Christ before returning. 

It is a matter of much regret that we 
have to report the discontinuance of our 
Branch Work in the past year. A combina- 
tion of circumstances rendered this decision 
necessary. Our North-east Branch Com- 
mittee, after a three months’ fruitless searcn 
for accommodation, were compelled to apan- 
acn the project for this year. An etrort, 
nowever, has been made to keep these poys 
cogether through the Hospital Service und 
meetings in the Central Building. It 1s our 
purpose to continue this work next fall if 
at all possible. The Branch at Point St. 
Charles was suspended pending the permarn- 
ent establishment of the work of the Assvu- 
elation in the new building. We hope that 
chis work also can be started in the fall. 

Last May Mr. R. H. Macdonald left the 
work, and during the summer months we 
were without a Secretary. In September 
Mr. C. M. Daggett came and took charge, 
and since then the work has gone on unin- 
cerruptedly. 

Viewed as a whole, our year’s work has 
peen very gratifying. Our object has been 
co make this department a distinctly boys’ 
organization, and in every way possible we 
have entrusted the boys with the responsi- 
pility of management. We have endeavored 
to discover new boys and to develop them in 
Christian service. A large number of the 
younger, as well as older boys have shown a 
remarkable aptitude for committee service. 

To sum up briefly :—

ber ist, 41%.

nasium, 73%.

EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


The total enrolment of individual mem- 
bers in the various classes was 463, an in- 
crease of 27 over last year. Eighteen sub- 
jects were taught, including new classes in 
physics and accountancy. Two classes for 
business boys were added with an enrolment 
of 29, making the total number of evening 
class students 492, and a total class enrol- 
ment of 547. 

A spring term, April 4 to June 10, has 
been started this year in bookkeeping, ele- 
mentary and advanced shorthand, mechani- 
zal drawing, German and French. Sixty- 
one members are enrolled, and the spring 
term will be a permanent feature. 

Additional equipment has been added, con- 
sisting of a large cupboard for the use of the 
drawing classes, twelve new desks, complet- 
ing the outfit for one of our class rooms, and 
a cupboard table with gas and water con- 
nections for the use of the classes in elec- 
wricity, chemistry and _ physics. We have 
oeen hard pressed many times to find ac- 
commodation for the several classes. 

Righty-four men wrote on the interna- 
tional examination, an increase of ten over 
last year. Forty-two passed the _ local 
examiners, and their papers were forwarded 
to the International Committee for final 
marking. The Orchestra, under the leader- 
ship of Mr. Chas. Reichling, met faithfully 
throughout the season. 

The following Lectures and Practical Talks 
nave been given during the season, many of 
which have been under the auspices of the 
Canadian Club :—

gave the closing address. 

The Bible Class for evening class students 
has been continued, with an enrolment of 
25. Twenty-two sessions were held, with a 
total attendance of 285, and an average of 13.

READING ROOM AND LIBRARY. 


The Reading Room contains 166 maga- 
zines, papers and periodicals, embracing all 
classes of the best publications; 126. of 
these were purchased, and 40 donated. The 
following publications have been added :— 
National Sportsman, Booklovers’ Magazine, 
Independent Review, Profitable Advertising, 
National Monthly of Canada, Resources of 
Canada. The Reading Room has been very 
well patronized by members. One week's 
actual count during the month of January 
showed 1,500 men in attendance. 

The Annual Sale of Magazines held in De- 
cember netted the sum of $94.70. 

The number of books circulated from the 
Library has not been so large as last year, 
although the number of readers semains 
about the same. Your Committee have de- 
cided to issue a printed catalogue to be used 
in addition to the present card system, be- 
lieving that the use of the library will be 
increased thereby. 

A very encouraging feature has been the 
numerous enquiries for books referring to 
some particular subject in which they were 
interested. 

The following books were purchased or 
donated during the year :—

PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 
During the past season the department 


conducted twenty-seven gymnasium classes 
each week, with a total attendance of 14,658, 
being a gain over the previous year of 460. 

The total number of men in gymnasium 
classes is 699, divided as follows :-—

There was an increase in the intermediate, 
students’, and senior business men’s classes, 
and a slight decrease in the junior business 
men’s class. The decrease in the attend- 
ance of the junior business boys’ class is due 
to an increase in the membership fee. The 
number of members examined during the 
year was 858—seniors, 230, and juniors, 128. 

Through the courtesy of Dr. H. Cushing, a 
ten weeks’ course in ‘First Aid to the In- 
jured” was given to members. This proved 
most helpful. 

The Committee-wish to thank Drs. Gilday 
and Cushing, who have rendered invaluable 
service as medical examiners. 


Leaders. 

The same esprit de corps spirit of the 
leaders has been a marked feature. Messrs. 
R. H. Macdonald and WD. McGavin have 
joined as ex-leaders. Their places have 
been filled by Messrs. S. R. Hall and C, D. 
Tweedie. The Gymnasium Exhibition at 
New Year’s Day reception was a success. 

At the opening of the Railroad Branch 


Building the leaders and advanced class 
members gave an exhibition. Mr. Geo. E. 


Winter has acted as instructor three nights 
a week in the Railroad Branch. 

The Corps have been brought together in 
a social way through the Annual Sleigh 
Drive, the Annual Banquet, and at the home 


of Mr. A. E. Smaill. The Corps is limited 
to 24 members. Number of exhibitions 
given, 3; average number of leaders en- 


gaged in leading, 12; number of leaders in 
examining room, 2; average attendance on 
Saturday night for practice in leading, 15. 


Hockey Club. 

The Hockey Club has had a successful sea- 
son. Two teams were picked to represent 
the club. The first team played in the 
Junior Amateur Hockey League, and made 
a creditable showing. The second team 
played in the Metropolitan League, and came 
out a tie for the championship in their sec- 
tion, but were defeated in the play-off, hav- 
ing won five and lost two matches. Be- 
sides the two hours a week at the Arena, 
one hour a week extra was rented at the 
Crystal Rink for the benefit of those who 
were not so fortunate as to be picked on the 


first and second teams. The club fee was 
raised this season. The membership num- 
bered 43, 


24 MEN OF MONTREAL 


Snowshoe Club. 
The Snowshoe Club doubled last year’s re- 


cord. Mention must be made of the 
Veteran’s Torchlight Procession, when one 
hundred members armed with smoking 


torches, winding like a huge snake in and 
out of the mountain paths, made a striking 
picture. A living pyramid was formed on a 
high bank, and a flashlight was taken, with 
excellent results. The members were en- 
thusiastic throughout the whole season. The 
membership was 65, with an average turn- 
out of 30; number of tramps, 21. 


Basket Ball. 

Basket Ball held the interest of a large 
number. Games were played on Thursday 
evenings, and were closely contested. The 
“Brits” proved themselves the senior cham- 
piens of the Association, and the “Beavers” 
won out the intermediate championship. 
They also defeated teams from Quebec, 
Westmount and the High School, winning 
the intermediate championship of the city. 
Seventy-two senior players, one hundred 
junior players. 


Tennis Club. 

The Tennis Courts, corner of Atwater Ave- 
nue and Dorchester Streets, were put in 
first-class condition at the beginning of the 
season, and were used by a large number of 
members during May and Jure, but owing to 
the extremely dry weather in July and 
August the attendance decreased. The club 
entered the Quebec League, and played home 
and home matches with Montreal and La- 
chine, winning from Lachine, and losing to 
Montreal. Large preparations are being 
made for the present season. 


Bowling Club. 


This has been the most successful season 
the club ever had. Our alleys were put in 
good condition in September, and with a 
number of improvements and additions we 
opened on the 4th of October. During the 
month of November we endeavored to enter 
a team in a bowling league, but were unable, 
as we only have two alleys, instead of three, 


the regulation.® But we made up four 
teams from the members, and arranged a 
schedule of games, which kept up the in- 


terest during November and December. 
During the season 4,140 tickets were sold 

and 4,013 strings bowled, an average of 143 

per week. A gold spoon was presented to 


the one each week making the highest single 
strings. The highest score was 267 and 


the lowest 194, the average 212. For our 
pin competition we gave a pin for the highest 
single string, one for the highest average 
for ten strings, and oue for the highest num- 
ber of spares made in ten _ strings. We 
played 17 matches and won 13; the highest 
score the team made was 3,154, and the total 
average was 2,909. Our financial report 


MEN OF 


25 


MONTREAL 


shows a balance on hand of $75.00, which 
was handed to the Association treasurer. 


Harrier Club. 

The Club met on May 5th. The first im- 
portant event was the meet with the 
M.A.A.A., held at their track on May 24th, 
when we entered three teams. The club 
continued to hold runs till about the middle 
of June, and then broke up for the hot 
weather. The average attendance of the 
club was 25, being the largest of any harrier 
club in the city. They started to run again 
in September at the Queen’s Park, and had 
some very pleasant runs along the river. A 
valuable cup was put up by the Honorary 


President, Mr. W. S. Leslie, for competition 


at the Field Day games. The successful 
team was composed of Messrs. Bond, Smith, 
Fleet, D’Albenas and Yuile, Mr. Bond’s time 
being 22 min., which was remarkably good. 
The Association offered to put up a cup to 
be the property of the club winning. Ata 
meeting of representatives from other clubs 
a meet for “The Championship of Montreal 
and District” was arranged to take place on 
the Lower Lachine Road on November 21st. 
Distance, five miles. The day was very cold, 
but the Y.M.C.A. won, the score being :— 
Y.M.C.A., 50 points; McGill, 45 points, and 
G.T.B.C., 25 points. Time. by Mr. A. W 
Lochead, of McGill. the winner, being 28.57. 
A supper was given to the team by the club. 
at which silver Association emblems were 
given to the members of the winning team. 


Athletics. 

Queen’s Park grounds were not secured 
until June 8th. Notwithstanding this delay, 
the club had a very successful season. La- 


ASSOCIATION SNOW SHOE CLUB 


crosse formed the chief attraction, and a 
number of match games were played. Run- 
ning, jumping, shot putting and hammer 
throwing also had their devotees. The 
membership numbered 26. The Annual Field 
Day was held on September 26th at Queen’s 
Park. There were 73 individual entries, as 
compared with 47 in 1902 and 64 in 1901. Two 
records were broken and one equalled. Dp. 
Mundy made the 100 yards in 10 3-5 secs., 
a noteworthy performance considering the 
yack was a turf one. He also equalled the 
record for 220 yards. G. Smith added 20 feet 
to his previous hammer throw record. A 
cup was put up for the best aggregate, and 
was captured by C. G. Higginson. A feature 
of the day was the four-mile Harrier Club 
team race for a silver cup presented by Mr, 
W. S. Leslie. 


Baseball. 
Owing to the uncertainty in regard te 
grounds, the club membership was small 


Financially we had a small surplus on the 
right side. An Amateur Baseball League 
was formed in the city, consisting of six 
clubs, and our club won the championship 
after an exciting contest. 

The Gymnasium Men’s Bible Study Club 
continued to be a strong factor throughout 
the department. The club held thirty seg. 
sions, with a total attendance of 1,166, an 
average of 39 per Sunday. Two special 
services were held on Christmas and New 
Year’s Day, at which Rev. W. D. Reid and 
Rev. J. L. Gilmour spoke. The club enrolled 
in its membership 85 men.

LADIES’ AUXILIARY. 


The Ladies’ Auxiliary has endeavored to 
render practical assistance in the work of 
the Association during the-past year as 
formerly. Sub-committees were appointed 
as follows :—Finance, Social, Furnishing, 
Flower and Junior, and have faithfully 
attended to the various duties assigned to 


them. These have included the assistance 
rendered by the ladies at the many social 
gatherings in the building, including the 
New Year's’ reception, the renewing of 
several articles of furniture in the parlors, 
replenishing of china, cutlery, linen, etc., in 
the kitchen. 

The Flower Committee has supplied 
flowers. each week for the building, and also 


sent them to sick young men, when infor med 
by the secretaries of such cases. 

The Junior Committee has assisted at 
the social gatherings in the work amongst 
the boys.

RAILROAD DEPARTMENT. 


The First Annual Report of the Railroad 
Department at Point St. Charles, Montreal, 
covers a period of one hundred days from 
the opening of the new building January 
21st,-1904, to May 1st of the same year. 

Regular religious services preceded the 
opening by several weeks, and have been 
eontinued every Sunday afternoon; one 
meeting for men only and another, a mixed 
meeting, which has been the means of in- 
teresting whole families. The attendance 
at these meetings has averaged 200 per 
week, 

Saturday night meetings have been held 
for men, which, while not great in numbers. 
have been the means of influencing several 
to begin the Christian life. 

Our two Bible Classes have been largely 
along the line of training in personal work, 
and conversions are not unusual. Cottage 
Prayer Meetings also preceded the opening 
of the building, and still continue. 

The attendance at the building has shown 
a very marked increase during the past 
month. At present we are using fifty beds, 
and expect soon to be obliged to place beds 
in the twenty-five unfurnished rooms. 


The physical work, under the leadership 
of Mr. George Winter, was conducted dur- 
ing the season in such a manner that it will 
undoubtedly serve as a strong drawing card 
for next fall’s work. 


On account of the lateness of the secson 
at the time of opening, we have conducted 
only one educational class, that in telegraphy, 
which will be continued six nights a week 
during the summer. 


We were able to close the year out of 
cebt, and it is the purpose of the manage- 
ment to so conduct the work, and the care 
‘of the building, that it will appeal not only 
‘to railroad men and to the young men of 
‘Point St. Charles, but. to others who are 
‘interested in the welfare of men, and who 
‘will so contribute to the maintenance of 
the work that there will be no necessity of 
limiting the usefulness and influence of our 
department.
